This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2021.00 “Fire Inspectors and Investigators” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope). Even within fire inspection and investigation, the differences are large: fire code inspection and hazard determination for buildings and premises, testing and acceptance testing of fire protection and alarm systems, verification of hazardous materials premises and permit issuance, scene examination, evidence collection, and cause analysis for fires and explosions, arson cases and courtroom testimony, and public fire education and special governance campaigns. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: the fire service or law enforcement background and years of experience required for the role, whether local or state-level inspector or investigator qualifications and certificates are required, whether the role carries inspection enforcement and permit issuance authority, the legal effect of investigation conclusions and the duty to testify, and the safety and personal protective requirements for site work.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious premises fire inspection assignment (premises type and use, building drawings and fire exit layout, list of fire protection and alarm systems, hazardous materials storage conditions, applicable fire code clauses, rectification deadlines and re-inspection arrangements). You are asked to write out the inspection items and the basis for each determination, the problems found and the rectification recommendations, the systems that require on-site testing and the testing methods, and which conclusions must be confirmed by the competent department or authorized personnel; mark which determinations require permits or enforcement authority to make.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to check code items one by one and keep written records, ability to communicate rectification requirements with owners and the public on site, and willingness to keep learning code updates and to bear evidence collection and testimony responsibilities. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to handle paperwork and code clauses, avoidance of conflict communication with owners, and treating a single inspection conclusion or one investigation result as a judgment about the entire occupation.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, legal, or safety conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make code verification and site work a long-term career: it requires memorizing and continually updating fire codes, inspecting and recording according to procedure, conducting investigation and evidence collection at fire and explosion scenes, and bearing enforcement boundaries and testimony responsibilities; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

Fire inspection and investigation work revolves around the cycle of “code verification—site inspection—rectification and permits—investigation and evidence collection—conclusions and reports”: first confirm the applicable regulations and technical standards and review building drawings and premises records; then conduct on-site inspections of buildings and premises according to checklists, verifying fire exits, electrical wiring, combustible material storage, and fire protection systems, and where necessary performing testing and acceptance testing of alarm, sprinkler, and detection systems; propose rectification recommendations for premises where hazards are found, follow up with re-inspections, and verify hazardous materials premises before issuing permits; when a fire or explosion occurs, examine the scene, collect and seal physical evidence, submit samples for testing, and analyze possible causes together with tests and interviews; then write inspection reports and investigation conclusions, testifying in court when necessary; at the same time carry out public fire education, evacuation drills, and special governance campaigns, continually updating code knowledge. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: premises inspection stresses inspection coverage and closed-loop rectification, fire system testing stresses test procedures and pass or fail determinations, hazardous materials permitting stresses condition verification and signing of responsibility, and fire investigation stresses the evidence chain and cause determination.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2021.00 “Fire Inspectors and Investigators”: inspect buildings to detect fire hazards and enforce local ordinances and state laws, or investigate and gather facts to determine the cause of fires and explosions.

Work context | Fire inspection and investigation work combines office and field: it involves reviewing drawings, writing reports, and organizing evidence, as well as working in buildings, premises, and fire scenes. O*NET work context shows that work schedules are mostly regular (85%), with 15% irregular; among weekly work hours, 41% exceed 40 hours, 44% are 40 hours, and 15% are less than 40 hours; 97% involve face-to-face discussions with people outside the organization every day, 93% involve telephone calls every day, and 90% involve email every day; 91% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined (61% extremely important, 30% very important); 31% have strict deadlines every day, 38% once a week or more, and 25% once a month or more; conflict situations occur every day for 12%, once a week or more for 34%, and once a month or more for 41%; 46% work outdoors in all weather every day, and 48% once a week or more; 33% wear common protective equipment every day; 16% are exposed to contaminants every day; the degree of automation of the work is 38% not at all automated, 31% slightly, and 24% moderately.

Main objects | Buildings and premises, building drawings and fire exit plans, fire protection and alarm and detection systems, hazardous materials storage and use facilities, fire and explosion scenes, physical evidence and samples submitted for testing, inspection records and investigation reports, and permits and rectification notices.

Collaboration | Collaboration with owners and premises managers, fire departments and enforcement personnel, building and engineering designers, hazardous materials organizations, inspection and testing bodies, prosecution and judicial authorities (testimony), and competent departments and the community public.

Tools and materials | Fire code and technical standard texts, checklists and enforcement documents, testing and detection equipment (alarm and sprinkler system testing, electrical and combustible gas detection), photography and evidence collection equipment, sealed containers and evidence bags, and computers and reporting systems.

Institutional basis | National and local fire codes, building fire protection codes and fire technical standards, hazardous materials management and permitting regulations, administrative procedure and enforcement document requirements, evidence preservation and courtroom testimony procedures, and occupational safety and health requirements.

Record requirements | Inspection records and rectification tracking records, investigation conclusions and evidence chain records, permit and approval records, testing and inspection records, and training and qualification records must be kept on file according to institutional rules.

Practice boundaries | The final determination of the cause of a fire or explosion, administrative penalties and permit decisions, and the legal conclusions of a case are not decided by an individual alone; matters involving enforcement, permits, evidence, and testimony must follow the competent department and statutory procedures, and this page does not provide legal or safe-operating advice.

Environment and pace | Site inspections require entering buildings, mechanical rooms, and storage areas, with possible exposure to dust, smoke, residue, and work at heights; when major fires or explosions occur, investigation work is intense and may require night and holiday response.

Region and scope | U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2021.00 does not map one-to-one onto mainland China's occupational classification; the mainland's fire supervision and fire investigation system, occupational qualifications, and enforcement authorization must be verified separately according to the local regulations.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2021.00 “Fire Inspectors and Investigators” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): inspect buildings to detect fire hazards and enforce local ordinances and state laws, or investigate and gather facts to determine the cause of fires and explosions. Specifically this includes: reviewing building drawings and verifying the applicable fire codes; patrolling buildings and premises according to checklists and verifying fire exits, electrical wiring, combustible material storage, and fire protection systems; performing testing and acceptance testing of alarm, sprinkler, and detection systems; verifying premises where hazardous materials are stored and used and issuing permits; writing inspection reports, violation records, and rectification recommendations and following up with re-inspections; when a fire or explosion occurs, examining the scene, collecting and sealing physical evidence, submitting samples for testing, and analyzing causes together with tests and interviews; testifying in court as needed; and carrying out public fire education, evacuation drills, and special governance campaigns while continually updating code knowledge.
entries.question: What do Fire Inspectors and Investigators mainly do?

entries.answer: Duties and authority differ: this occupation conducts premises inspection, system testing, hazardous materials permitting, and investigation of fire and explosion causes under fire codes and may testify in court; firefighters focus mainly on firefighting, rescue, and emergency response; fire protection engineers focus mainly on technical solutions for fire protection systems and building fire protection design; emergency management directors focus mainly on emergency plans, resource coordination, and interagency coordination; building and construction inspectors focus mainly on building structure, construction quality, and general code inspection; police and patrol officers focus mainly on public order maintenance and criminal enforcement; private detectives and investigators conduct civil and commercial investigations on commission and do not hold fire enforcement authority; and compliance specialists focus mainly on internal institutional compliance review and process oversight.
entries.question: How does it differ from firefighters and fire protection engineers?

entries.answer: U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-2021.00 “Fire Inspectors and Investigators”: interest code RCI, Job Zone Three (requiring medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to <7.0), not marked as Bright Outlook (projected average growth of 3% to 4% for 2024—2034). Definition notes: wages, employment, and growth are on the exact occupation definition (2025 median hourly wage $36.50, median annual wage $75,920; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles are about 46,530, 58,690, 95,120, and 118,750 USD / year respectively; 2024 employment about 14,700; average annual job openings about 1,500). BLS OOH separately gives the occupational group (fire inspectors, including forest fire inspectors) 17,600 employed in 2025, 6% growth for 2025—2035, about 1,900 average annual openings, and a median annual wage of $73,680, which is on a group basis and marked at each occurrence in the body text. The education survey has published the leading items (postsecondary certificate 27%, some college no degree 26%, high school diploma or equivalent 23%), the remaining items are not published, and this page does not fill them in.

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (requiring medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to <7.0). Work context shows that work schedules are mostly regular (85%), with 15% irregular; among weekly work hours, 41% exceed 40 hours, 44% are 40 hours, and 15% are less than 40 hours; 97% involve face-to-face discussions with people outside the organization every day and 93% involve telephone calls every day; 91% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined; 31% have strict deadlines every day and 38% once a week or more; conflict situations occur every day for 12% and once a week or more for 34%; 46% work outdoors in all weather every day; 33% wear common protective equipment every day; the degree of automation of the work is 38% not at all automated, 31% slightly, and 24% moderately. The work combines office and field, and when major fires or explosions occur it may require night and holiday response.

entries.answer: The more accurate judgment is that steps such as code searching, drawing comparison, report drafting, and record archiving will be taken over by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation and an upward shift in the center of responsibility. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, that the share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations is relatively low, and that technical feasibility does not mean agencies have already adopted it; on-site determination, evidence selection, conclusion determination, and signing responsibility must be borne by authorized personnel, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change, not that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

BLS OOH separately gives the occupational group (fire inspectors, including forest fire inspectors) a 2025 median annual wage of $73,680 (hourly $35.42), and gives forest fire inspectors and fire prevention specialists a May 2025 median annual wage of 56,870 USD, both on a group-internal definition. The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution of the employed, not a starting wage; OEWS is on an employed-person definition, and BLS has not published a readable figure for this occupation's industry-specific wages.

entries.answer: The accuracy of inspection determinations and the evidentiary responsibility for investigation conclusions are borne by the personnel carrying them out; the final determination of the cause of a fire or explosion, administrative penalties and permit decisions, and the legal conclusions of a case must be made by the competent department through statutory procedures. Site work must be carried out in accordance with occupational safety and health requirements, and evidence preservation and testimony proceed according to procedures; matters involving enforcement, permits, evidence, safety, and testing must be confirmed by the competent department or authorized personnel. When using tools, tool outputs do not constitute an enforcement basis or conclusion, and sensitive premises and case file information must not be disclosed externally or submitted to unrelated parties. subject.name: Fire Inspectors and Investigators
subject.summary: Inspect buildings to detect fire hazards and enforce local ordinances and state laws, or investigate and gather facts to determine the cause of fires and explosions: includes conducting premises inspections and hazard determinations under fire codes, testing and acceptance-testing fire protection and detection systems, checking premises where hazardous materials are stored or used and issuing permits, examining fire and explosion scenes and collecting physical evidence for laboratory submission, writing inspection and investigation conclusion reports, and carrying out public fire education and evacuation drills.
